questions.question: What is the Java type system and why does it exist? It defines the set of primitive and reference types that every variable must belong to, enabling compile-time type safety and predictable memory layout.
questions.title: Java Syntax Basics
questions.direct_answer: The Java type system is the compile-time framework that classifies every variable, expression, and parameter as either a primitive type or a reference type. It exists because a statically typed language catches type errors before the program runs, and because fixed-size primitives guarantee platform-independent memory layout. The eight primitive types (byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean) are stack-allocated and passed by value, while reference types (classes, arrays, interfaces) are heap-allocated and passed by reference value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can list the eight primitive types with their sizes and default values, and explain the difference between primitive and reference types.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the size of char (16-bit, not 8-bit) or thinking boolean has a defined size in the spec, or forgetting that primitives are passed by value.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain autoboxing and unboxing, the wrapper class cache for Integer (-128 to 127), and why Java chose fixed-size primitives for cross-platform consistency.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Java is a statically typed language, meaning every variable must be declared with a type before use. The type system divides all values into two categories: primitive types and reference types. There are exactly eight primitive types -- byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean -- each with a fixed size that is guaranteed to be the same on every platform, unlike C where sizes can vary. Reference types include classes (String, custom objects), arrays, and interfaces; they are allocated on the heap and accessed via references. The compiler enforces type compatibility at compile time, catching most type errors before the program ever runs.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: Java has exactly eight primitive types with platform-independent sizes: byte (8-bit), short (16-bit), int (32-bit), long (64-bit), float (32-bit), double (64-bit), char (16-bit Unicode), and boolean (true/false). Each primitive has a corresponding wrapper class (Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character, Boolean) in java.lang that allows primitives to be used in generic collections and reflection. Autoboxing automatically converts a primitive to its wrapper, and unboxing does the reverse, both with potential performance implications in tight loops. Reference types are allocated on the heap, default to null, and are garbage collected when no longer reachable. Primitives are stack-allocated (for local variables), have type-specific default values (0 for numbers, false for boolean), and are always passed by value.

sections.title: Primitive Types, Wrappers, and Autoboxing
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: Primitives are fast and memory-efficient because they are stack-allocated and have no object header overhead, but they cannot be used in generic collections (List<int> is illegal) and have no methods. Wrapper classes bridge this gap via autoboxing, but the boxing overhead can be significant in performance-critical loops. Java's fixed primitive sizes guarantee cross-platform consistency at the cost of not being able to use native word sizes for efficiency on 64-bit platforms. When memory is critical (e.g., large arrays), prefer primitives over wrappers to avoid the 16-byte object header per element.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Java has exactly 8 primitive types with platform-independent sizes: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean.
Primitives are stack-allocated, passed by value, and default to 0 (numbers) or false (boolean).
Each primitive has a corresponding wrapper class that enables use in generics and collections.
Autoboxing converts primitives to wrappers automatically, and unboxing does the reverse.
Reference types are heap-allocated, default to null, and are accessed via references.
Widening conversions are implicit and safe; narrowing conversions require an explicit cast and may lose data.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Java's type system is statically typed, meaning every variable must be declared with a type before use. There are two categories: primitives and reference types. The eight primitives are byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean, each with a fixed size that is the same on every platform. This design exists so the compiler can catch type errors at compile time and so memory layout is predictable and portable. Each primitive has a wrapper class like Integer or Double that allows it to be used in generic collections through a feature called autoboxing. Primitives are stack-allocated and passed by value, while reference types like String and arrays are heap-allocated and default to null. In performance-critical code, I prefer primitives over wrappers because each wrapper object carries a 16-byte header and boxing in loops can really add up.

questions.question: What are the 8 primitive data types in Java and what are their sizes?
questions.title: 8 Primitive Data Types in Java with Sizes
questions.direct_answer: Java has **8 primitive types**: `byte` (1 byte), `short` (2 bytes), `int` (4 bytes), `long` (8 bytes), `float` (4 bytes), `double` (8 bytes), `char` (2 bytes), and `boolean` (typically 1 bit). They are **not objects** — they live on the stack, hold values directly, and can't be `null`.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing float/double sizes or forgetting that char is 2 bytes in Java (not 1 like C)

sections.title: Java's 8 Primitive Data Types
sections.content:
A **data type** is a label that tells Java what kind of value a variable can hold. When you write `int score = 95;`, the `int` is the data type — it tells Java this variable will hold a whole number.

Java has **8 built-in data types** called **primitives**. They are called primitive because they are the simplest values in Java — not objects, just raw values stored directly in memory. They cover everything a program commonly needs: whole numbers, decimal numbers, a single character, and a yes/no flag.

The 8 types fall into four groups:
- **Whole numbers** — `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long` — for counting things (age, score, quantity)
- **Decimal numbers** — `float`, `double` — for prices, measurements, averages
- **A single character** — `char` — one letter like `'A'` or one symbol like `'@'`
- **True/false** — `boolean` — for yes/no decisions and conditions

In everyday code, you will reach for `int` for almost every whole number and `double` for almost every decimal. The other types (`byte`, `short`, `float`) are for special cases where memory matters — like processing thousands of sensor readings. `long` is for large numbers that overflow `int`, such as timestamps in milliseconds.

Two things interviewers always check:
1. Java's `char` is **2 bytes** — not 1 byte like in C. Java uses Unicode to support every language, so each character needs the extra space.
2. Primitives can **never be `null`**. They always hold a value. When you declare `int count;` as a field, Java automatically sets it to `0`. If you need a variable that might be absent, use the wrapper class: `Integer` instead of `int`.

sections.title: All 8 Primitive Types at a Glance
sections.content:
| Type | Size | What it holds | Common example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `byte` | 1 byte | Whole number −128 to 127 | `byte age = 25;` |
| `short` | 2 bytes | Whole number −32,768 to 32,767 | `short year = 2024;` |
| `int` | 4 bytes | Whole number ±2 billion **(default)** | `int score = 95;` |
| `long` | 8 bytes | Very large whole number *(needs `L`)* | `long userId = 9876543210L;` |
| `float` | 4 bytes | Decimal, less precise *(needs `f`)* | `float temp = 36.6f;` |
| `double` | 8 bytes | Decimal, more precise **(default)** | `double price = 9.99;` |
| `char` | 2 bytes | Single Unicode character | `char grade = 'A';` |
| `boolean` | ~1 bit | `true` or `false` only | `boolean isLoggedIn = true;` |

sections.title: The 4 Families of Primitive Types
sections.content:
If someone asks you to name all 8 primitives, grouping them by family is much easier than trying to recall a flat list.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["8 primitive types"] --> W["Whole numbers"]
    P --> D["Decimal numbers"]
    P --> C["Single character"]
    P --> B["True / false"]
    W --> W1["byte · 1 byte"]
    W --> W2["short · 2 bytes"]
    W --> W3["int · 4 bytes (default)"]
    W --> W4["long · 8 bytes (needs L)"]
    D --> D1["float · 4 bytes (needs f)"]
    D --> D2["double · 8 bytes (default)"]
    C --> C1["char · 2 bytes · Unicode"]
    B --> B1["boolean · true / false"]
```

Notice the two defaults: `int` for whole numbers, `double` for decimals. Those are the two you will write in almost every program.

sections.title: Wrong — missing literal suffixes
sections.content:
```java
// These look fine but won't compile
long bigNumber = 9999999999;   // ERROR: Java reads this as int — it overflows
float price = 3.99;            // ERROR: 3.99 is a double by default, can't fit in float
```
Java reads whole-number literals as `int` and decimal literals as `double`. If you want `long` or `float`, you have to tell Java explicitly.

sections.title: Right — add L for long, f for float
sections.content:
```java
long bigNumber = 9999999999L;  // L tells Java: treat this literal as long
float price = 3.99f;           // f tells Java: treat this literal as float
char grade = 'A';              // single quotes, 2 bytes in Java (not 1 like C)
boolean isActive = true;       // only true or false — never null
```
The `L` and `f` suffixes are the two most common compile errors for freshers on their first day.

sections.title: All 8 Primitives in One Program
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking `char` is 1 byte like in C**: Java's `char` is **2 bytes** because it stores a UTF-16 Unicode code unit, not an ASCII byte — anyone coming from C or C++ gets this wrong.
- **Mixing up `float` and `double`**: `float` is 4 bytes (~7 significant digits), `double` is 8 bytes (~15). Reaching for `float` to "save space" on a single value buys nothing and quietly loses precision — `double` is the default for a reason.
- **Forgetting the literal suffix**: `long big = 10000000000;` does not compile — the literal is read as an `int` and overflows. Write `10000000000L`. Same trap with `float f = 3.14;`, which needs `3.14f`.
- **Assuming a primitive can be `null`**: `int x = null;` is a compile error. Primitives always hold a value — switch to the wrapper (`Integer`, `Double`) only when "absent" is a state you genuinely need to represent.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`char` is 2 bytes, not 1** — Java stores a UTF-16 code unit, so a `char` holds any Unicode character; developers coming from C assume 1 byte and miscount memory.
- **`int` and `double` are the defaults** — integer literals default to `int`, decimal literals to `double`; reach for the other types only with a concrete reason.
- **`long` needs `L`, `float` needs `f`** — `long big = 10000000000;` overflows `int` and won't compile; the missing suffix is the classic day-one error.
- **Primitives can never be `null`** — `int x = null;` is a compile error; use `Integer` or `Double` only when "absent" is a real state you must model.
- **Fields default, locals don't** — instance and static primitives auto-initialize (numbers to `0`, `boolean` to `false`, `char` to the null character); using a local variable before assigning it is a compile error, not a silent zero.
- **`float`/`double` can't represent money exactly** — both are binary floating-point, so `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`; use `BigDecimal` for currency.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The cleanest way to answer is to **group them rather than recite eight names**. Four are whole-number types — `byte`, `short`, `int`, and `long` — at one, two, four, and eight bytes. Two are decimals — `float` at four bytes, `double` at eight. Then `char` at two bytes, and `boolean`. In real code you reach for `int` for almost every whole number and `double` for almost every decimal; the rest are for special cases, like a `long` for a timestamp or an ID that overflows `int`.

Two details sharpen the answer. **Java's `char` is two bytes, not one like in C**, because it stores Unicode — that catches people out. And **primitives can never be `null`**; they hold the value directly, which is part of why they're faster than objects. I'd also mention defaults: an `int` field starts at zero and a `boolean` at false, but **a local has no default**, so reading one before you assign it won't compile. Those points — the two-byte `char` and no nulls — are what show you've actually written Java, not just memorized the list.

questions.question: What is the difference between instance variables, local variables, and static variables in Java?
questions.title: Instance vs Local vs Static Variables in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Instance variables** belong to an object (heap), get default values, and each object has its own copy. **Local variables** live inside a method (stack), have **no defaults**, and must be initialized before use. **Static variables** belong to the class (method area) and are shared across all instances.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java memory model and variable scoping rules
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking local variables get default values — they don't; the compiler errors on an uninitialized local variable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention where each lives (stack vs heap vs method area) and the thread-safety implications of static variables

sections.title: Where You Write the Declaration Decides Everything
sections.content:
A **variable** in Java is a named place that holds a value. Java has three kinds of variable — **instance**, **local**, and **static** — and which kind you get depends only on *where in the code you write the declaration*.

These three kinds exist because different values need to live for different lengths of time and belong to different owners. Some data belongs to one specific object, some belongs to a whole class, and some is just temporary scratch work inside a single method. The three kinds cover those three needs.

Here is how to tell them apart. Write the declaration inside a method and it's a **local variable**. Write it in the class body, outside any method, and it's an **instance variable** (also called a field). Write it the same way but put the word `static` in front, and it's a **static variable**.

What changes between them is *who owns the value* and *how long it lives*, and that maps straight onto where Java keeps the variable in memory. A **local variable** is scratch paper for one method call: it lives on the **stack**, appears when the method starts, and vanishes the moment the method returns — so every call gets a fresh copy, which is why locals are naturally thread-safe. An **instance variable** belongs to one object and sits on the **heap** beside it; make three `Student` objects and you get three separate `name` fields, each living as long as its object. A **static variable** belongs to the class itself — there is exactly **one** copy, kept in the **method area** and shared by every object and every thread for the whole program. That single shared copy is perfect for a counter of objects created, and risky if many threads change it without synchronization.

> The rule freshers trip on: instance and static fields auto-initialize to defaults (`0`, `false`, `null`), but a **local has no default** — read it before assigning a value and the code will not even compile.

sections.title: Instance vs Local vs Static at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Instance|~Per object|on the heap|default-initialized|one copy per object
blue|Local|~Inside a method|on the stack|NO default value|must initialize first
emerald|Static|~Per class|method area|shared by all instances|lives the whole program
rose|Watch out|~Statics + threads|need synchronization|locals are thread-safe|no instance access in static methods

sections.title: Instance vs Local vs Static Variables
sections.content:
| Aspect | Instance variable | Local variable | Static variable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scope | Belongs to an object | Inside a method/block | Belongs to the class |
| Memory | Heap (with the object) | Stack (method frame) | Method area (shared) |
| Default value | Auto (0/false/null) | None — must initialize | Auto (0/false/null) |
| Lifetime | As long as the object | Until the method returns | Entire program runtime |
| Access | Via object reference | Only in declaring scope | Via class name or instance |

sections.title: Why the Compiler Rejects an Uninitialized Local
sections.content:
The most common surprise is that a local variable does not start at zero. The compiler refuses to guess a starting value and forces you to assign one first.

```java
void process() {
    int count;                 // local variable: NO default value
    System.out.println(count); // COMPILE ERROR: count might not be initialized
}
```

This is a *compile* error, not a runtime crash — Java catches it before the program ever runs. A field in the same situation would silently be `0`, which is exactly why people expect the same here and get burned.

sections.title: The Fix: Locals Initialize, Fields Default for Free
When to Use Each Variable Type
sections.content:
Pick the kind by who should own the value:

- **Instance variables** — for state that varies between objects, like a `User`'s name, email, age.
- **Local variables** — for temporary work inside a method, like loop counters or intermediate results; they're short-lived.
- **Static variables** — for data shared across instances: a connection pool, app config, a counter of objects created, or `static final` constants.

If two objects should share a value, make it `static`; if each needs its own, make it an instance variable.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting local defaults**: `int count; System.out.println(count);` won't compile — locals must be initialized.
- **Accessing instance variables from static methods**: not allowed — static methods belong to the class, not an object.
- **Thread safety with statics**: static variables are shared across threads; modifying them without synchronization causes race conditions.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Instance** — per object, on the heap, default-initialized.
- **Local** — inside a method, on the stack, no defaults, must initialize.
- **Static** — per class, method area, shared across instances and threads.
- **Memory model** — heap vs stack vs method area.
- **Initialization** — only locals cause a compile error if used uninitialized.
- **Thread safety** — statics need synchronization; locals are stack-isolated.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The fastest way to keep these straight is to notice **you never declare the kind** — where the line sits decides it. A variable inside a method is local, one in the class body is an instance variable, and adding `static` makes it belong to the class instead of any object.

What really separates them is **ownership and memory**. Each object gets its own copy of every instance variable, sitting on the heap and living as long as the object. A `static` variable has just one copy in the method area, shared by every object and every thread for the program's whole life — which is why a static counter works, and also why mutating one from multiple threads needs synchronization. Local variables live on the stack, exist only while the method runs, and each call gets a fresh one, so **they're naturally thread-safe**.

The detail that catches people is **initialization**. Instance and static fields auto-default to zero, false, or `null`, but **a local has no default at all** — declare `int count` and read it before assigning, and the compiler stops you cold. That's a compile error, not a silent zero. So I think of it as instance for per-object state, static for shared state, and local for throwaway work inside a method.

questions.question: What will this code print — and why? `int a = 5; int b = a; b = 10; System.out.println(a);`
questions.title: Java Primitive Copy vs Reference Gotcha
questions.direct_answer: It prints **`5`**. Primitives in Java are **copied by value** — `int b = a` gives `b` its own copy of `5`. Changing `b` to `10` has no effect on `a`; they are completely independent variables.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands pass-by-value and the difference between primitives and objects in Java
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing this with object references where two variables can point to the same object
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast with object reference behavior — if a and b both referenced the same object, mutating via b would affect what a sees

sections.title: Why It Prints 5: Assignment Copies the Value, Not a Link
sections.content:
When you assign one primitive variable to another in Java — like `int b = a;` — Java copies the **value** across. It does not tie the two variables together. So this code prints **`5`**.

Why does it work that way? A primitive variable holds its number directly, right inside its own slot in memory. There is no link or pointer to share, so the only thing Java *can* do on assignment is copy the number itself.

Now read the lines the way Java does. `int a = 5;` puts the number `5` into a box called `a`. `int b = a;` does **not** connect the boxes — it reads whatever value is currently in `a` (which is `5`) and copies that number into a brand-new box called `b`. From that instant, `a` and `b` are strangers that merely happen to hold the same number. So when `b = 10;` runs, only box `b` changes; nothing ever wired `a` to `b`, so `a` still holds `5`.

The everyday picture is a photocopy: scribble on the copy and the original is untouched. For all 8 primitive types, assignment makes a fresh, independent copy — that is **copy by value**.

The reason interviewers love this question is the contrast they hope you'll draw. If `a` and `b` were object references — say two `ArrayList` variables — then `b = a` would copy the *arrow*, not the list, and both names would point at the same object. A change through `b` would absolutely show up through `a`.

> Primitives copy the value; reference variables copy the link.

The same trap appears in method calls: pass a primitive in and the method gets its own copy, so it can never change the caller's variable — which is why you `return` a value to send one back out.

sections.title: Value Copy vs Reference Share at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Primitives|~Copied by value|int b = a copies 5|fully independent|changing b leaves a at 5
blue|Objects|~Copied by reference|both point to one object|shared state|mutating via one shows in the other
emerald|Method calls|~Also pass-by-value|primitive copied in|change inside is local|return to send a value back
rose|Why it matters|~No aliasing for primitives|stack-isolated|thread-safe locals|predictable debugging

sections.title: Primitives: Two Boxes That Never Talk to Each Other
sections.content:
Here is the exact code from the question. Watch how `b` moves on its own while `a` stays put.

```java
int a = 5;
int b = a;   // b gets a COPY of 5
b = 10;      // changing b does not touch a
System.out.println(a); // 5
```

There is no shared storage between `a` and `b` — each `int` owns its own slot, so the only way to change `a` is to assign to `a` directly.

sections.title: Objects: Two Names Pointing at One Thing
sections.content:
```java
var listA = new java.util.ArrayList<String>();
listA.add("Alice");
var listB = listA;   // listB points to the SAME object as listA
listB.add("Bob");    // mutation visible through listA too
System.out.println(listA.size()); // 2
```
Primitives copy the value; object variables copy the reference — that's the whole difference.

sections.title: The Same Rule Explains Method Arguments
Why This Matters in Real Code
sections.content:
Value copying shows up in several everyday spots:

- **Passing primitives to methods** — the method gets a copy, so it can't change the caller's variable; you must `return` a modified value.
- **Loops** — it matters when copying a counter.
- **Debugging** — two primitives with different values are guaranteed independent, unlike object references that may share state.
- **Thread safety** — local primitives are inherently safe because each thread has its own stack frame.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting a link**: `int b = a;` doesn't connect the variables — they're separate.
- **Confusing with objects**: `List<String> listB = listA;` makes both point to the same list, so changes via one are visible through the other.
- **Thinking parameters are references**: passing an `int` and changing it inside doesn't affect the original — use a `return`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Value copying** — primitive assignment copies the value; variables are independent.
- **No shared state** — changing `b` after `int b = a` doesn't touch `a`.
- **Method parameters** — primitives are copied in; changes stay local.
- **Contrast with objects** — references share the same object.
- **Stack allocation** — each primitive gets its own stack slot.
- **Thread safety** — local primitives are inherently thread-safe.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
**It prints `5`** — and that's the whole point of the question. When you write `int b = a`, Java doesn't wire the two variables together; it reads the value in `a`, copies that number into a fresh slot for `b`, and walks away. So changing `b` to `10` touches only `b` — `a` was never connected, so it stays `5`. **It's like photocopying a page**: scribbling on the copy never changes the original.

Where I'd show I actually understand it is **the contrast with objects**. If `a` and `b` were two references to the same `ArrayList`, then `b = a` would copy the arrow, not the list, and adding through `b` would show up through `a`. **Primitives copy the value; reference variables copy the link** — and that same rule is why passing an `int` into a method can't change the caller's variable, since the method just gets a copy. **Java is always pass-by-value**; for objects, the value being copied just happens to be the reference.

questions.question: What does the final keyword do when applied to a variable in Java?
questions.title: final Variables in Java — Constants and Immutable References
questions.direct_answer: **`final`** on a variable means it can be **assigned only once**. For primitives the value can't change; for object references the **reference** can't be repointed — but the object's internal state can still be mutated. It's the reference that's final, not the object.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the distinction between a final reference and an immutable object — a classic gotcha
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking final makes an object immutable — it only prevents reassignment of the reference, not modification of the object's contents
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clarify the difference between a final reference and a truly immutable object, and mention final instance variables must be initialized in the constructor or at declaration

sections.title: Why a final Reference Still Lets You Mutate the Object
sections.content:
The `final` keyword on a variable means one simple thing: once you give it a value, you can never change that value again. Put `final` in front of a variable and you make exactly one promise to the compiler: *I will assign this once and never again.* Try to reassign it later and the code won't compile. That's the entire idea.

For a primitive this is the plain "constant" behaviour you'd expect. `final int MAX = 100;` means `MAX` is `100` and stays `100` for good.

For an **object reference**, there's a twist that catches almost every fresher. Take `final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();`. What's locked here is the **reference** `names` — the arrow pointing at that one list. You can never repoint `names` at a *different* list. But `names.add("Alice")` is completely legal, because adding an item changes the list's *contents*, not which list `names` points to.

> The one-line rule worth memorizing: **`final` stops reassignment, it does not stop mutation.**

A house address written in permanent ink can't be changed, yet you can still renovate the rooms inside. If you want an object whose contents genuinely can't change, that's a separate idea — immutability — and you get it from things like `List.of(...)` or `String`, never from `final` alone.

One more rule the compiler enforces: a `final` **instance variable** must be assigned exactly once, either at its declaration or in every constructor — you cannot leave it unset and fill it in later.

sections.content:

blue|On primitives|~Value is locked|final int MAX = 100|a true constant|can't change
emerald|On references|~Reference is locked|can't repoint|but the object CAN mutate|names.add() still works
rose|True immutability|~Needs more than final|no setters + final fields|List.of(), String|design the class

sections.title: The Trap: final List Is Not an Immutable List
sections.content:
Here is the line of reasoning that bites people: "it's `final`, so the list can't change." Watch what the compiler actually allows versus what it blocks.

```java
final java.util.List<String> names = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
names.add("Alice"); // ALLOWED — final locks the reference, not the contents
// names = new java.util.ArrayList<>(); // COMPILE ERROR: can't reassign
```

The `add` compiles fine; only the reassignment is rejected. So a `final` collection can still grow, shrink, or be cleared by anyone holding the reference — `final` gave you a stable name, not a frozen object.

sections.title: The Fix: Lock the Binding and the Object Separately
final on Fields, Locals, and References Together
When to Use final
sections.content:
Reach for **`final`** in a few clear cases:

- **True constants** — `final double PI = 3.14159;`.
- **Parameters** — to prevent accidental reassignment.
- **Instance variables set once during construction** — an ID, a timestamp.
- **Collections** — when you want a stable reference but still modify contents.

Many teams use `final` liberally because it makes code more predictable and catches reassignment bugs early.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing final reference with immutability**: `final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();` still allows `items.add(...)`. `final` only blocks reassigning `items`.
- **Not initializing final instance variables**: they must be set at declaration or in every constructor, or it's a compile error.
- **Thinking final freezes the object globally**: another method holding the same reference can still mutate the object.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Single assignment** — `final` variables are assigned exactly once.
- **Primitives vs references** — value locked vs reference locked.
- **Mutation allowed** — a `final` reference's object can still change.
- **True immutability** — needs no setters and final fields (e.g., `String`).
- **Instance variables** — must be initialized at declaration or in the constructor.
- **Constants** — combine `static final` with ALL_CAPS naming.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The thing that trips people up here isn't what `final` does — it's how far it reaches. **`final` makes a variable assign-once**: bind it, and any later reassignment is a compile error. For a primitive that's the obvious constant behaviour — `final int max = 100` and `max` is 100 forever.

The twist is with object references. When you write `final` `List` of `String` `names` = new `ArrayList`, **what's locked is the reference** — the arrow pointing at that list. You can never repoint it at a different list, but `names.add` is completely legal, because that mutates the list's contents, not which list `names` points to. So **`final` stops reassignment; it does not stop mutation**. A `final` reference is not an immutable object. If you want contents that genuinely can't change, that's a separate decision — `List.of`, or a class with no setters and `final` fields, the way `String` is built.

There's also a rule the compiler enforces: **a `final` instance variable has to be assigned exactly once**, either at its declaration or in every constructor path — you can't leave it unset. In practice I use `final` liberally on fields and parameters, because it documents that a value shouldn't change and lets the compiler catch an accidental reassignment before it ever becomes a bug.

questions.question: What is the var keyword in Java and when should you use it?
questions.title: var Keyword and Local Type Inference in Java 10
questions.direct_answer: The **`var`** keyword (Java 10) is **local type inference** — the compiler infers the variable's type from the initializer. It works **only for local variables with an initializer**, never for fields, parameters, return types, or a `null` initializer. Java stays statically typed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of modern Java features and understanding that var doesn't make Java dynamically typed
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking var means dynamic typing like JavaScript — Java is still statically typed; the type is fixed at compile time
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that var reduces boilerplate with generics, and explain where it cannot be used (fields, parameters, null initializer)

sections.title: var Infers the Type — It Doesn't Make Java Dynamic
sections.content:
The `var` keyword lets you declare a local variable without writing its type — you write `var`, and Java works out the type from the value you assign. It was added in Java 10 to cut down on repetition. One thing to clear up right away, because interviewers fish for it: `var` does **not** turn Java into JavaScript or Python — it doesn't loosen the type system at all.

Look at this line: `ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<String>();`. You wrote `ArrayList<String>` twice on one line — once on the left, once on the right. That repetition is noisy, and Java 10 added a fix: the **`var`** keyword. Write `var names = new ArrayList<String>();` and the compiler reads the right-hand side, sees it's an `ArrayList<String>`, and fills the type in for you. That is all `var` does.

Crucially, the type is still decided at **compile time** and then locked forever. After `var count = 0;`, the variable is permanently an `int` — try `count = "hello";` later and it won't compile. Java is exactly as statically typed as before; you just wrote the type once instead of twice.

Every restriction falls straight out of how it works. Because the compiler needs the right-hand side to infer from, `var` only works for **local variables you initialize on the same line**. It can't be used on fields, method parameters, or return types, and `var x = null;` fails because `null` gives the compiler nothing to infer from.

> Reach for `var` when the type is obvious at a glance; spell the type out when it isn't.

sections.title: var at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|var|~Local type inference|Java 10+|compiler reads the right side|still statically typed
blue|Allowed|~Locals with initializer|var x = 42;|for (var o : list)|great with generics
emerald|Not allowed|~No fields/params/returns|no null initializer|no declaration without init|type locked at compile time
rose|Use it|~When type is obvious|cuts boilerplate|readability over brevity|don't make readers guess

sections.title: Why var Needs Something to Infer From
sections.content:
Both of these look harmless but fail at compile time, and the reason is the same in each case — there's nothing for the compiler to read a type from.

```java
var user = null;  // COMPILE ERROR: can't infer a type from null
var temp;         // COMPILE ERROR: var needs an initializer
```

`null` belongs to every reference type, so it points at no single one; and a bare `var temp;` gives the compiler no right-hand side at all. `var` is only ever as smart as the initializer you hand it.

sections.title: The Fix: Give var a Clear Right-Hand Side
sections.content:
Once the initializer pins down a type, `var` works cleanly — and the inferred type is just as rigid as if you'd written it yourself.

```java
var message = "hello";                               // inferred String
var count = 0;                                       // inferred int
var map = new java.util.HashMap<String, Integer>();  // cuts generic boilerplate
// count = "text";  // still statically typed — this would NOT compile
```

The commented line is the proof: `count` is locked to `int` the moment it's inferred. `var` saved you keystrokes, not type safety — that last line is rejected exactly as it would be without `var`.

sections.title: The Four Places var Is Banned — and Where It Shines
When to Use var
sections.content:
A quick rule of thumb for when `var` helps and when it hurts:

- **Use `var`** when the type is obvious from the right-hand side — `var service = new OrderService();`.
- **It shines** with verbose generics and in loops — `for (var order : orders)`.
- **Avoid it** when the initializer is a method call whose return type isn't obvious — `var result = service.process(data);` makes readers guess.

The guideline: if someone must hover in an IDE to know the type, spell it out.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking var is dynamic typing**: once `var count = 5;` infers `int`, you can't assign a `String` later — the type is locked.
- **Using var with null**: `var user = null;` fails — no type to infer.
- **Overusing var**: `var x = calculate();` with a non-obvious return type hurts readability.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Local type inference** — compiler infers the type from the initializer.
- **Still static** — the type is fixed at compile time.
- **Locals only** — not fields, parameters, or return types.
- **Needs an initializer** — and it can't be `null`.
- **Great with generics** — cuts verbose declarations.
- **Readability over brevity** — use it when the type is obvious.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The mistake to head off right away is **thinking `var` makes Java loose like JavaScript** — it doesn't. `var`, added in Java 10, is purely **local type inference**: when you write `var` `orders` = new `ArrayList` of `Order`, the compiler looks at the right-hand side, sees it's an `ArrayList` of `Order`, and fills that type in for you. The variable is permanently that type. Try to reassign it to a `String` later and it won't compile — **Java is exactly as statically typed as before**, you just wrote the type once instead of twice.

The restrictions all fall out of how it works. Because the compiler needs the initializer to infer from, **`var` only works on local variables you initialize on the same line**. No fields, no method parameters, no return types, and `var x = null` fails because `null` gives it nothing to work with.

Where it earns its keep is verbose generics — `var` `byStatus` = new `HashMap` of `OrderStatus` to `List` of `Order` reads far cleaner than spelling that out twice. But I'd only reach for it when the type is obvious from the right side. If someone has to hover in their IDE to know what `var result` is, I spell the type out. **The rule I follow is readability over brevity**.

questions.question: What is the difference between int and Integer in Java?
questions.title: int vs Integer — Primitive vs Wrapper and Autoboxing
questions.direct_answer: **`int`** is a **primitive** — it holds the value directly, lives on the stack, is fast, and can never be `null`. **`Integer`** is a **wrapper class** — a real object on the heap that wraps an `int`, so it *can* be `null`. The compiler converts between them automatically: `int → Integer` is **autoboxing**, `Integer → int` is **unboxing**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the primitive/object divide and why wrappers exist for generics and collections
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that unboxing a null Integer throws a NullPointerException, and using == instead of .equals() to compare Integer objects
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that List<int> is illegal so wrappers exist for generics, and mention the Integer cache (-128..127) as the reason == sometimes works and sometimes doesn't

sections.title: int Holds the Number; Integer Is an Object That Wraps It
sections.content:
In Java, `int` and `Integer` both hold a whole number — write `int age = 30;` or `Integer age = 30;` and either one stores `30`. That much every beginner already half-knows. The real question is *what kind of thing* each one is.

`int` is a **primitive**: it holds the value directly inside its own slot, lives on the stack, is fast, and can **never be `null`**. `Integer` is a **wrapper class** — a genuine object that lives on the heap and simply wraps a single `int` inside it. Because it is an object, an `Integer` reference *can* be `null`, carries a little memory overhead, and comes with helper methods like `Integer.parseInt("42")`.

Why does Java even need a wrapper? Because generics and the collections framework only work with **objects**, never with primitives. `List<int>` does not compile — you have to write `List<Integer>`. That single rule is the biggest reason wrappers exist: they let primitive values travel through `List`, `Map`, `Optional`, and every other generic type.

To keep that from being painful, the compiler converts for you. Turning an `int` into an `Integer` is **autoboxing**; turning an `Integer` back into an `int` is **unboxing**. So `Integer x = 5;` is really `Integer x = Integer.valueOf(5);`, and `int y = x;` is really `int y = x.intValue();` — you rarely write those calls yourself.

> The gotcha interviewers wait for: unboxing a `null` `Integer` throws a `NullPointerException` at runtime.

`Integer total = null; int n = total;` compiles cleanly and then blows up, because the hidden `total.intValue()` runs on `null`. A related subtlety — the `Integer` cache reuses objects for values −128 to 127, which is why `==` between two `Integer`s sometimes works and sometimes fails — is its own topic; for now, just compare with `.equals()`, not `==`.

sections.title: int vs Integer Side by Side
sections.content:
| Aspect | `int` (primitive) | `Integer` (wrapper) |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A raw value | An object wrapping an `int` |
| Memory | Stack, holds value directly | Heap, holds a reference |
| Can be `null`? | No — always has a value | Yes — reference can be `null` |
| Default value | `0` | `null` |
| Works in generics? | No — `List<int>` is illegal | Yes — `List<Integer>` |
| Has methods? | No | Yes (`parseInt`, `compareTo`, ...) |
| Compare with | `==` (value compare) | `.equals()` (not `==`) |
| Speed | Faster, no allocation | Slower, object overhead |

sections.title: Primitive, Wrapper, and the Conversions Between Them
sections.content:
amber|int|~Primitive value|lives on the stack|can't be null|fast, no allocation
blue|Integer|~Wrapper object|lives on the heap|can be null|works in generics
emerald|Autobox / unbox|~Compiler converts|int to Integer = autobox|Integer to int = unbox|valueOf and intValue
rose|Watch out|~null unboxing = NPE|use .equals not ==|Integer cache -128..127|prefer int unless null needed

sections.title: The NullPointerException Hiding Inside an Innocent Assignment
sections.content:
This looks like a plain copy from one number variable to another. It compiles without a single warning — and then crashes the moment it runs.

```java
Integer total = null;     // a wrapper reference can legally be null
int count = total;        // RUNTIME: NullPointerException
System.out.println(count);
```

The trap is invisible because the conversion is invisible. `int count = total;` is silently `int count = total.intValue();`, and calling `intValue()` on `null` throws. The compiler can't catch it — a `null` `Integer` is perfectly valid right up until something tries to unbox it.

sections.title: The Fix: Check for null Before You Unbox
sections.content:
Once you know unboxing is a hidden method call, the fix is obvious — guard against `null`, or stay in wrapper land until you're sure there's a value.

```java
Integer total = null;
int count = (total != null) ? total : 0;  // safe: only unbox when not null
System.out.println(count);                // prints 0
```

The ternary unboxes `total` only when it actually holds a value, falling back to `0` otherwise. The broader rule: any place a `null` `Integer` can meet an `int` — assignments, arithmetic, `if (flag)` on a `Boolean` — is an unboxing crash waiting to happen, so treat wrapper values as possibly-`null` until proven otherwise.

sections.title: Autoboxing in Action Inside a List
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Unboxing a `null` wrapper**: `Integer x = map.get("missing"); int y = x;` throws a `NullPointerException` because `get` returned `null` and unboxing called `intValue()` on it. Always treat a wrapper from a map, query, or API as possibly `null`.
- **Comparing `Integer` with `==`**: `==` compares object references, not values. It *appears* to work for small numbers because of the `Integer` cache (−128 to 127 are shared objects), then fails for `1000 == 1000`. Use `.equals()` or unbox to `int` first.
- **Using `Integer` everywhere by habit**: a wrapper allocates an object and can be `null`, so prefer plain `int` for counters, loop variables, and fields that always have a value — reach for `Integer` only when you genuinely need `null` or generics.
- **Boxing in hot loops**: `Integer sum = 0; for (...) sum += x;` re-boxes on every iteration, creating thousands of throwaway objects. Use an `int` accumulator instead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Primitive vs object** — `int` holds the value on the stack; `Integer` is a heap object wrapping an `int`.
- **null** — `int` can never be `null`; `Integer` can, and that's the whole point of using it.
- **Why wrappers exist** — generics and collections need objects, so `List<int>` is illegal but `List<Integer>` works.
- **Autoboxing / unboxing** — the compiler inserts `Integer.valueOf()` and `intValue()` for you automatically.
- **NPE gotcha** — unboxing a `null` `Integer` throws a `NullPointerException` at runtime, not compile time.
- **`==` vs `.equals()`** — compare `Integer` values with `.equals()`; `==` only works by luck inside the −128..127 cache.
- **Default to `int`** — use the primitive unless you specifically need `null` or generics.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The cleanest way to put it is that **`int` is the raw value and `Integer` is an object that wraps that value**. `int` lives on the stack, holds the number directly, and can never be `null`; `Integer` lives on the heap, can be `null`, and carries helper methods. The reason the wrapper exists at all is generics — **collections only hold objects**, so you can't write `List<int>`, you write `List<Integer>`. To make that painless, the compiler **autoboxes** an `int` into an `Integer` and unboxes it back automatically, inserting `valueOf` and `intValue` for you.

The detail I'd make sure to land is **the null trap**: unboxing a `null` `Integer` throws a `NullPointerException` at runtime, because that hidden `intValue()` call runs on `null` — and it compiles fine, so nothing warns you. I'd also note you compare `Integer`s with `.equals()`, not `==`, since `==` only seems to work for small cached values. So my rule is: **default to `int`**, and reach for `Integer` only when you genuinely need `null` or generics.
